idiom_name: Per-tap AsyncStream fan-out from an actor with a bufferingNewest drop policy
implementation_notes: Hand-rolled fan-out on the stdlib primitives - Swift ships no tee for value streams. An actor owns the tap registry: each tap is an (AsyncStream, Continuation) pair from AsyncStream.makeStream(bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(N)). The interposed publish forwards the original message to the primary receiver first, then calls continuation.yield(message) per tap; yield returns immediately without blocking for awaiting consumption (SE-0314), so analyzer speed never backpressures the flow - the only producer cost is a bounded actor hop plus a memcpy-sized enqueue on the cooperative thread pool, no thread per tap. Copy semantics: what yield takes is the value - independent only for Sendable structs with value-typed storage; Array/Dictionary/String are copy-on-write and class-typed fields inside the message stay shared, so the tap payload must be an immutable Sendable struct or a serialized snapshot. Overflow policy is explicit and built in: .bufferingNewest(N) drops when the buffer is full, yield reports it as .dropped(Element) or .terminated, and the tap counts both into a visible drop counter; .unbounded (makeStream's default) buffers without limit and must be chosen deliberately. Each tap gets its own stream and exactly one iterator - iterators of one stream race and share termination - the analyzer drains it with for-await inside its own Task and detaches via continuation.finish() without touching sender or receiver. When an existing AsyncSequence is what you must observe, use swift-async-algorithms share(bufferingPolicy:) (AsyncAlgorithms 1.1+): every iteration makes independent forward progress with the same values, a bounded policy lets a lagging side drop, and the default .bounded(1) backpressures the upstream - a real tradeoff the classic tap avoids. In a Combine-based stack use multicast { PassthroughSubject() }, which delivers each upstream event once to many subscribers once connect() is called.
pitfalls: YieldResult is @discardableResult: with a bounded policy, a yield onto a full buffer silently discards the copy and merely returns .dropped(Element) - code that ignores yield's return loses all analyzer traffic without a trace, so count .dropped and .terminated into a metric.

.unbounded is the default buffering policy of makeStream and buffers 'without imposing a limit on the number of buffered elements': a lagging analyzer grows the buffer until memory runs out, hiding overload that a bounded .bufferingNewest(N) would expose as counted drops.

Yielding to a stream already finished or cancelled is a no-op returning .terminated - traffic sent to a torn-down tap vanishes with no error, so remove terminated continuations from the registry or the tap keeps 'receiving' forever while every copy is lost.

The copy is value semantics, not isolation: Array, Dictionary and String are copy-on-write and class-typed fields of a struct message stay shared references - Apple's Array documentation shows a mutation through a shared class instance remaining 'visible from either array' - so an analyzer inspecting a message with reference-typed members mutates or observes the primary's live state unless the payload is immutable Sendable or serialized.

Never share one stream or channel between taps: SE-0314 warns that multiple iterators of an AsyncStream 'may produce an unexpected series of values' and concurrent iteration is a programmer error, SE-0406 records that AsyncThrowingStream fatalError's when a second iterator suspends and that one consumer's cancellation terminates all consumers, and AsyncChannel's send delivers each element to exactly one waiting consumer - attaching a second subscriber steals messages from the primary receiver.
